title: Judith (Judith 8–13)
hook: a widow rebukes the elders for testing God and saves her city

segments.voice: Yesterday, Tobias and Sara began their marriage on their knees, and Raguel filled in the grave. Your line was pray together first.

A small hill town called Bethulia is under siege. The general Holofernes has surrounded it with a huge army and cut off the springs. The cisterns are running dry, and children are fainting in the streets. The people shout at their leaders: surrender. Better slaves and alive than watch our children die of thirst. So the chief elder, Ozias, makes a deal. Hold out five more days. If God hasn't helped us by then, we'll open the gates. It even sounds like faith. And a widow in the town hears about it.
screen: `A HILL TOWN UNDER SIEGE.` → `THE SPRINGS CUT OFF.` → `FIVE MORE DAYS, THEN SURRENDER.`

segments.voice: Her name is Judith, which simply means a Jewish woman, a woman of Judea. Her husband had died of sunstroke at the barley harvest, and for over three years she'd lived as a widow, fasting and praying, wealthy and respected; nobody, the book says, spoke an ill word of her. She sends for the elders and doesn't soften it. Who are you to put God to the test? You've set a deadline for the mercy of the Lord. God isn't a man, to be threatened or bargained with. If he wants to save us, he can, in his own time. Then she tells them she has a plan, and not to ask what it is. She prays, trades her widow's clothes for her finest, and walks out the town gate with her maid, straight into the enemy camp. She tells Holofernes she's come to help him win, and he is charmed. On the fourth night he throws a banquet, drinks more than he ever has, and falls asleep. Alone in the tent, Judith takes his own sword and kills him. She carries his head home in her food bag, and the leaderless army breaks and runs. It's a hard, bloody story, and the book doesn't look away. It also doesn't read like a chronicle: it opens with Nabuchodonosor as king of the Assyrians, reigning in Nineveh, and some readers, Catholic scholars among them, take details like that as signs of a story told to teach. What it teaches is clear: when the leaders gave up, a widow didn't.
screen: `JUDITH: A WOMAN OF JUDEA.` · `YOU SET A DEADLINE FOR GOD'S MERCY.` · `INTO THE ENEMY CAMP.` · `A STORY TOLD TO TEACH.` · then, large: `WHEN THE LEADERS GAVE UP.`

segments.voice: Think of a place you belong where the people in charge have quietly given up: a team, a parish committee, a family, a town that has set a deadline for hope. Ask what one respectful, honest sentence you could say to them, the way Judith called the elders and told them the truth. If you pray, ask for her courage.
Judith. The widow of Bethulia who rebuked the elders for putting God on a deadline, and then went out and saved her city. Today's word.
Your line: a widow saved the city. Faith that wouldn't set God a deadline. That's day four hundred thirty-nine.

screen: `DAY 439 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: IN THE HAND OF GOD.`

howItsDone: Catholics hear Judith in the Liturgy of the Hours and at Mass, and the Church's liturgy applies the praise given to Judith, blessed above all women, to the Virgin Mary.

chat.says: What's the Book of Judith actually about? Just a woman with a sword?
options: A widow who refused to put God on a deadline, and acted when the leaders gave up.
A widow who sat out the five-day deadline praying until God sent rain.
A queen who led Israel's army into battle against the Assyrians.

notes: Editor review (2026-10-01): 'many scholars' and the flat 'which history doesn't match' / 'deliberate anachronisms' replaced with 'some readers, Catholic scholars among them' in teach, myth and trapdoor; the text's own detail (Nabuchodonosor king of the Assyrians in Nineveh, Judith 1:5) kept.
All of Judith is paraphrased; the Douay (Vulgate) and Greek differ in verse numbering and detail.
Judith's husband Manasses died of sunstroke at barley harvest (8:2–3); widowhood 'three years and six months' in Vulgate, 'three years and four months' in Greek: 'over three years' used. Confirm.
Holofernes killed on the fourth day/night (Greek 12:10); confirm the detail as told.

Anachronism statement (Nebuchadnezzar as king of Assyria in Nineveh): standard in Catholic scholarship (e.g. introductions in the NAB, Jerusalem Bible). Confirm wording 'many scholars, Catholic ones among them'.
Liturgical use of Judith 13:18/13:23 and 15:9–10 for Mary (e.g. 'Tu gloria Ierusalem'): confirm.
The violence is described plainly but without detail; confirm tone is acceptable for the app.
